<reason>Side A wins by establishing that the proposition concerns marginal spending on perishable physical infrastructure versus easily added digital tools, and by successfully defending against the exclusion critique: common spaces allow peripheral participation without mandatory attendance, while "first" does not mean "only" existing digital services. A also caught B's concession that digital tools "coordinate" community, arguing one cannot amplify a hollowing-out campus. B's strong inclusion case was weakened by a clipped Rebuttal 1 and A's distinction between scheduled events and open spaces.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 answer distinguishing open common spaces from scheduled societies, which neutralized B's "mandatory physical presence" critique by showing low-barrier access without opt-in or disclosure.</best_rebuttal>
